abstractText:
The human head houses many important physiological signals such as brain signals (EEG), facial muscle signals (EMG), eye signals (EOG), etc. which have tremendous value in inferring the user's mental, physiological, and physical states. In addition, it also serves as an ideal body part for applying brain stimulations. However, most of the existing head-based sensing and stimulation methods are cumbersome, intrusive, and expensive, mostly suitable only for stationary and short-term usages such as in clinics or hospitals. This project aims to fill that gap by enabling a novel form of wearable sensing and actuating systems that can unobtrusively, continuously, comfortably, and simultaneously sense a multitude of head-based physiological signals and actuate to stimulate the brain while remaining minimally visible to the public. While the well-accepted form factors for wearable devices are watches, glasses, and other kinds of body-worn form factors, this work takes a drastically different approach, an ear-worn sensing and actuation approach (called Earable Systems) to tame a problem that has long hindered the deployment of head-based wearable systems, namely user acceptance, by making the wearable devices more socially acceptable and less visible to the public. 

The intellectual merit of this project stems from the key research activities. The activities include: formulating multiple head-based signal propagation models to and from human ears using superposition principle of wave propagation; developing algorithms, experimental hardware blocks, analytical models, and software libraries for sensing individual head-based physiological signals; developing closed-loop stimulation techniques, associated hardware, analytical tools, and safety guidelines for effective and safe just-in-time brain stimulation from the ears; and evaluating Earable Systems and the proposed platform in-lab for a compelling and practical application. 

This project's broader impacts stem from an integrated program of education, research and outreach that will translate the research results into demonstrations and hands-on experiences for under-served middle school students and local teachers through lab visits and summer workshops.  It will also provide a unique interdisciplinary education for future engineering and healthcare workforce.  It will also provide insight to future healthcare technologies through two Open Online Courses (MOOCs) for clinicians and undergraduate engineering students.  And, both undergraduate and graduate students will be involved in advanced interdisciplinary healthcare projects using Earable Systems concepts. The research has the potential to translate scientific discovery and technical knowledge into beneficial commercial products through industry outreach and internships.

projectOutComesReport:
The objective of this CAREER project was to lay a scientific foundation for robust, efficient, and personalized ear-worn sensing and actuation systems—called the Earable platform—for long-term, unobtrusive, closed-loop healthcare and real-time brain-computer interactions. Human ears are close to the brain, eyes, and facial muscles, making ear-based sensors minimally visible and highly acceptable to users. Our focus was on three objectives: (1) refining a wearable headband for accuracy, comfort, and usability; (2) validating the system for sleep monitoring and epileptic seizure detection; and (3) building an on-chip AI framework for resource-constrained wearable hardware.A foundational accomplishment was the development of a novel ear-worn sensing device. We identified that electrodes placed on the squamous and mastoid areas of both ears can capture brain, eye, and facial muscle signals using only two sensing electrodes, enabling a lightweight, low-cost, and discreet wearable. We developed adaptive filtering, novel adaptive gain control, and a Three-fold Cascaded Amplifying technique (3CA) to mitigate motion artifacts and environmental noise. The device was refined into a headband with ultrasoft materials, a retractable magnetic lockstrap for universal fit, a simplified control interface, and over 12 hours of battery life. This culminated in the FRENZ Brainband, a consumer-grade device equipped with dry-active nanomaterial-based electrodes, photoplethysmography, an inertial measurement unit, microphone, speakers, and LED arrays for closed-loop health monitoring and stimulation.For sleep monitoring, we validated the platform in a large-scale study collecting data from 377 patients over 883 sessions alongside polysomnography (PSG). We showed that Earable can robustly categorize sleep stages using algorithms that compare favorably with manual assessments by three sleep professionals, and can provide effective personalized audio stimulation to reduce sleep onset time. The technology was commercialized as the FRENZ Brainband, now distributed in over 40 countries. Manufacturing capacity reached 1,760 devices per month (35-day lead time), scalable to 5,280 per month.For epilepsy detection, we conducted clinical trials involving 33 patients and 9 clinicians at the Epilepsy Monitoring Unit at UT Southwestern Medical Center, achieving up to 93.5% seizure detection accuracy. In collaboration with UMass Amherst, we demonstrated the ability to capture seizure biomarkers using a compact ear-based device.The project also enabled additional applications: focus-tracking and cognitive monitoring deployed in the Japan XPRIZE study; in-ear blood pressure monitoring (eBP) using adaptive arterial pressure; pain quantification (Painometry) via facial muscle bioimpedance; microsleep detection achieving over 87% precision for known subjects; and hands-free human-computer interaction through tongue-teeth and head-based sensing.For on-chip AI, we developed an uncertainty-aware wearable event detection system based on evidential theory and a cascade ML framework with early exits for efficient inference. Evaluations demonstrated up to 864% faster inference, 857% greater power efficiency, 55% storage savings on prevalent MCUs, and 22% improvement in uncertainty quantification. This framework enables real-time, dependable event detection across a wide range of wearable hardware.Research outcomes were published at leading venues including ACM MobiCom, MobiSys, SenSys, UbiComp, IEEE PerCom, IEEE Transactions on Mobile Computing, Communications of the ACM, PLOS Digital Health, and Scientific Reports. Notable publications include eBP (MobiCom 2019, Best Paper Award), WAKE microsleep detection (MobiSys 2020), Painometry (MobiSys 2020), FaceSense (UbiComp 2021), UR2M uncertainty-aware framework (PerCom 2024), and closed-loop acoustic stimulation for sleep (Scientific Reports 2023). Over 10 patents were filed covering ear-worn biosignal sensing, blood pressure, pain quantification, respiration monitoring, and activity detection. The platform received CES Innovation Awards in 2023, 2024 and 2025, a Global Luxury Lifestyle Award for "Best Wearable Sleep Improvement Innovation in the USA," and a MedTech Breakthrough Award in 2025.The project resulted in a spin-off company, Earable Inc., which commercialized the FRENZ Brainband. By project close, the company had established professional manufacturing, distribution in over 40 countries, and a commercial partnership with Tonino Lamborghini. Three software tools were released: an EEG data collection tool, a focus-tracking algorithm, and a B2B data collection application.The project provided extensive training opportunities. Graduate students and postdoctoral researchers gained experience in wearable design, embedded systems, signal processing, ML on microcontrollers, and clinical research. The technology was integrated into courses at CU Boulder (Wearable/Mobile Systems for Health) and Dartmouth (Neuro Technology for AI, Spring 2025). Findings were disseminated through keynotes at MobiSys 2025, CES 2025, HLTH 2024, and invited talks at MIT, Stanford, Princeton, CMU, Oxford, Google, and others. Collaborations included UMass Amherst, University of Montana, Cardiff University, CU Denver, Children's Hospital Colorado, CU Hospital, and UT Southwestern.In conclusion, this CAREER project advanced ear-worn sensing from early prototypes to a validated, commercially deployed health technology platform. The research demonstrated that minimal ear-based sensors can reliably capture diverse physiological signals for sleep monitoring, seizure detection, cognitive tracking, blood pressure, pain quantification, and microsleep detection. The on-chip AI framework enabled efficient ML inference on constrained hardware. The commercialization of the FRENZ Brainband, multiple industry awards, and scalable manufacturing demonstrate a clear pathway from fundamental research to real-world impact in personalized healthcare and digital health.
